newsitem.title: TANZANIA: Rwanda genocide tribunal told defendant too ill.
newsitem.headline: Rwanda genocide tribunal told defendant too ill.

text.p: The International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda, sitting for the first time since May, considered a request on Wednesday that a Rwandan Hutu charged with genocide be released on medical grounds.

Tribunal officials told Reuters that Belgian defence lawyer Luc de Temmerman was meeting judges and prosecutors in this northern Tanzanian town to argue in camera that his client Georges Rutaganda was too ill to stand trial.
The tribunal was created by the United Nations after the genocide in Rwanda between April and June 1994, when up to one million minority Tutsis and pro-opposition Hutus were killed.
Its mandate is to try the top planners and perpetrators of the genocide, not the tens of thousands of ordinary killers.
The tribunal, which has yet to begin trials, has indicted only 21 people and has only three in its custody. They face a maximum penalty of life imprisonment if found guilty.
De Temmerman wants Rutaganda released so he can be treated for his undisclosed ailment.

"The judges and prosecutors are meeting to decide whether he should be released or not," tribunal spokeswoman Beatrice Lacoste told Reuters. She said he was "very ill" and the court would announce its decision later on Wednesday.

The tribunal is supposed to open its first trial on Thursday with Jean Paul Akayesu, aged 43 and also accused of genocide. But Akayesu's lawyers have sought an adjournment on procedural and other grounds. That application will be heard on Thursday.

Rutaganda, a former agricultural engineer and businessman, is accused of being the second vice-president of the national committee of the Interahamwe, a militia group which played a leading role in the 1994 genocide.

He was charged in late May with eight counts of genocide, crimes against humanity (extermination), crimes against humanity (murder) and violations of Article 3 of the Geneva Conventions. Rutaganda, like two others held at Arusha, pleaded not guilty.

Rutaganda is accused of arming Hutu extremists in April 1994 and ordering the murder of Tutsi civilians with machetes, guns, grenades and by drowning. The prosecution alleges some victims were forced to dig their own graves.
Rutaganda is also charged with distributing weapons to Interhamwe militia and stationing militiamen near his office in Kigali to catch ethnic minority Tutsis.
He is charged with participating in an attack on a technical school where thousands of unarmed Tutsi men, women and children were sheltering and taking part in a second attack on survivors.
The six-page indictment says in June 1994 Rutaganda ordered people to bury the bodies of victims to conceal his crimes.

The killings broke out in the tiny country after the assassination of Hutu president Juvenal Habyarimana on April 6, 1994. Angry followers including the army, militia and Hutu civilians hunted down Tutsis -- blamed for Habyarimana's death -- and Hutus opposed to his military rule.
In Rwanda, where the death penalty exists for the most guilty, there are 80,000 detainees waiting to be charged, tried or released.

The tribunal says 10 indictees are in custody -- three in Arusha, two in Belgium, one in Switzerland and four in Cameroon. Kenya last week arrested a Rwandan Hutu businessman, Obeid Ruzindana, on a warrant said to have been signed by the tribunal.
